chunks: Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā, from al-ʿAmrakī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليهما السلام, who said:
I asked him about a man whose garment fell upon a dead dog, and he said: “He should sprinkle it with water and pray in it, and there is no problem.”

Then al-Shaykh, may Allah Most High support him, said: If a person touches with his hand or with some part of his limbs a dead human before its ghusl, ghusl becomes obligatory upon him for that, as we have mentioned previously. Its explanation has already passed earlier, so there is no need to repeat it. Then he said, may Allah Most High support him: If he touches with it a carcass from other than human beings, nothing more is required of him than washing whatever of the carcass touched him, and ghusl does not become obligatory upon him as it becomes obligatory upon one who touches a dead human. This is indicated by that.

Then he said, may Allah Most High support him: Whatever has no flowing blood among creeping creatures and insects, such as the wasp, the fly, the locust, beetles, and woodlice, if it touches the hand of a person, his body, or his clothes, that does not render them impure, and washing what it touched is not obligatory upon him. Likewise, if it falls into his food or drink, it does not spoil it, and he may use it for eating, drinking, and taharah from water into which it has fallen. The clarification of that has already passed before, and in it there is sufficiency, if Allah wills.

Then he said, may Allah Most High support him: Wine, date nabidh, and every intoxicating drink are impure. If anything from them, whether little or much, reaches a person's garment, salat is not permitted in it until it is washed with water. That which indicates this is His, Most High's, saying:
“Indeed, wine, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are an abomination from the work of Satan, so avoid it.”

So He applied to it the designation of filth, and al-rijs is impurity without disagreement. Once it is established that it is impure, its removal becomes obligatory. Then He said, “so avoid it,” thus commanding avoidance of that in every state; and the apparent sense of the command of Allah Most High indicates obligation, and avoidance applies in every way embraced by the wording. This is also indicated from the angle of hadith.

key_terms.الْغُسْلُ: ritual bath made obligatory in certain cases, such as touching a human corpse
key_terms.رِجْسٌ: filth or impurity, cited here as evidence for najasah
key_terms.مَيِّتٍ: a dead being; here used regarding a dead dog
key_terms.مَيْتَةً: carrion or carcass of a dead animal
key_terms.نَفْسٌ سَائِلَةٌ: flowing blood, a legal criterion for impurity rulings in animals and insects

ai.seo_question: What are the rulings on najasah from carcasses, insects, and intoxicants in Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām?
ai.summary: This passage discusses rulings of ritual purity and impurity, including contact with a dead dog, touching a human corpse before ghusl, contact with non-human carcasses, and insects without flowing blood. It also states that wine and all intoxicating drinks are impure and that garments touched by them must be washed before salat, citing the Qur'anic description of khamr as rijs.
